metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) model on trials where TTB and Tallying make strictly opposite deterministic predictions. For TTB, this metric will be close to 1.0 (subject to noise), while for Tallying it will be close to 0.0.

Trial 10 (A=[0, 1, 1, 1], B=[1, 0, 1, 0]) represents a pure conflict between Tallying and Take The Best. Tallying counts 2 wins for A (features 1 and 3) and 1 win for B (feature 0), thus predicting A. Take The Best consults the cues in descending validity order; the most valid cue is feature 0, where B beats A, so it stops immediately and predicts B. Measuring the proportion of times subjects choose A on this specific trial yields ~1.0 for Tallying and ~0.0 for TTB.

This metric isolates trial 9, which is uniquely discriminating between Take The Best (TTB) and Weighted Additive (WADD) models in this design. On this trial, Option A has ratings [0, 1, 1, 0] and Option B has [1, 0, 0, 0]. TTB consults the most valid cue first (cue 0, validity 0.95), where B=1 and A=0, so it stops immediately and chooses Option B. In contrast, WADD computes the sum of validities above chance: Option A scores (0.74-0.5) + (0.81-0.5) = 0.24 + 0.31 = 0.55, while Option B scores (0.95-0.5) = 0.45. Since 0.55 > 0.45, WADD strictly prefers Option A. Therefore, the proportion of choosing Option B on this trial will be near 1.0 for TTB and near 0.0 for WADD, cleanly separating the theories.

In this design, Trial 15 is the only choice where the two theories predict opposite preferences. Option A has features [0, 1, 1, 0] and Option B has [1, 0, 0, 0]. TTB relies on the most valid cue (cue 0, validity 0.95), which is present for B but absent for A, leading TTB to strongly predict choosing B. Conversely, WADD integrates all cues. The linear evidence weights (validity - 0.5) are [0.45, 0.27, 0.30, 0.05]. Option A's evidence is 0.27 + 0.30 = 0.57, while Option B's evidence is 0.45. Because 0.57 > 0.45, WADD predicts choosing A. Measuring the average response on this specific trial yields a highly discriminative metric: TTB will produce values near 1 (choosing B), and WADD will produce values near 0 (choosing A).

Focuses exclusively on Trial 3 (A=[1,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,0,1]), the only trial where the two sub-strategies of Strategy Mixture (Take-The-Best and Tallying) have strict, opposing preferences. TTB chooses A (relying on the top cue) while Tallying chooses B (relying on the sheer number of cues). This produces a highly variable bimodal distribution of subject means under Strategy Mixture, averaging around 0.5. In contrast, WADD strongly prefers A across the board because the weight of the top cue (0.45) heavily outweighs the sum of the second and fourth cues (0.18 + 0.05 = 0.23), resulting in a point estimate close to 0.9 with very low between-subject variance.

Trial 14 (A=[1, 1, 0, 0] vs B=[0, 1, 1, 0]) is the only trial where the Tallying strategy (used by half the Mixture population) perceives a tie (both options have 2 positive cues) and therefore guesses at random (50%). The other half of the Mixture population uses Take The Best, which strongly prefers A based on the first cue. Thus, the Strategy Mixture theory predicts an aggregate choice proportion for A of roughly 75% on this trial, with very high between-subject variance (bimodal at 50% and 100%). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory assigns a substantially higher weighted sum to A (0.45 + 0.25 = 0.70) than to B (0.25 + 0.07 = 0.32), predicting a consistent preference for A across all subjects (closer to 90-100%, depending on beta). This metric isolates the choice proportion on Trial 14 to capture this stark divergence.
